texts.preamble: Dr.Santosh Singh vs State on 6 March, 2017 Author: P.K. Lohra Bench: P.K. Lohra High Court Of Judicature For Rajasthan At Jodhpur S.B.Criminal Misc(Pet.) No. 778 / 2015 Dr. Santosh Singh S/o Shri Chhotey Lalji, by caste Gahlot, resident of B-25, Narsingh Vihar, Gas Godam Road, Jodhpur, (Ex Chief Medical & Health Officer, Jodhpur). ----Petitioner Versus State of Rajasthan ----Respondent _____________________________________________________
texts.facts: The facts, in brief, giving rise to this petition are that in the year 1999, petitioner was working as Chief Medical and Health Officer, Jodhpur and as such was empowered to give written consent and authorize someone to launch prosecution by resorting to Section 20 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (for short, 'Act of 1954') (since repealed). It so happened that Food Inspector was Om Prakash Kalla took sample of Mustard Oil on (2 of 6) [CRLMP-778/2015] 25.09.1999, which after analysis was found adulterated. After completion of the entire process, the matter was placed before the petitioner for his written consent to file complaint against the accused person for offence punishable under Section 7/16 of the Act of 1954. During trial, Om Prakash Kalla appeared in the witness-box and the petitioner examined as a prosecution witness besides other witnesses. Learned trial Court, on conclusion of trial, acquitted the accused but, taking into account some contradictions in the statements of petitioner as well as Om Prakash Kalla, directed the Assistant Public Prosecutor to file complaint against petitioner and Om Prakash Kalla for filing wrong complaint and giving contradictory statements in the Court. Pursuant to the directions of the Court, Assistant Public Prosecutor filed a complaint against the petitioner and Om Prakash Kalla under Section 193 IPC read with Section 195 and 340 Cr.P.C. before learned trial Court. Dr.Santosh Singh vs State on 6 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/122661242/ 1 Being aggrieved by the said order, the petitioner filed a revision petition before learned revisional Court but the learned revision Court declined to interfere with the order of cognizance. Therefore, in that background, petitioner has approached this Court.
texts.arguments: Mr. P.N. Mohanani, learned counsel for the petitioner, submits that mere contradictions in the statements of two witnesses cannot constitute offence of perjury within the meaning of Section (3 of 6) [CRLMP-778/2015] 193 IPC. It is argued by learned counsel that the basic ingredient for constituting offence of perjury is deliberate and conscious attempt by an individual to give false statements or to file false affidavit before the Court. Learned counsel for the petitioner would contend that role of the petitioner was limited to the extent of giving written consent or authorizing a person to file complaint and, therefore, even considering the limited role of the petitioner under Section 20 of the Act of 1954, he cannot be prosecuted for offence under Section 193 IPC. In substance, submission of the learned counsel is that order of cognizance by the learned trial Court and its affirmation by the learned revisional Court is per se vulnerable and cannot be sustained. In support of his contention, learned counsel has placed reliance on a decision of Supreme Court in Ashok Kuamr Aggarwal Vs. Union of India & Ors.:2014 Cri.L.J. 1213. Per contra, learned Public Prosecutor has vehemently opposed the petition and has urged that the order of cognizance passed by learned trial Court has been affirmed by revisional Court, therefore, it is not desirable to exercise second power of judicial review in the matter. Learned Public Prosecutor has further submitted that serious contradictions in the statements of petitioner and Om Prakash Kalla have rightly persuaded the learned trial Court to order prosecution of the petitioner and other incumbent for offence of perjury while passing the verdict of acquittal.
